c.v: One reason for each. Four wheels are a count fixed at compile time, so the elements can sit inside the object with no allocation. The route is appended to and walked in order, which is what one contiguous block does best. The parameters must come out sorted, and only an ordered container gives that without sorting for every print. The message ids need only "have I seen this one?", which a hash set answers without keeping any order. The commands leave from the front, and a vector has no O(1) way to remove its first element.
You pass with five defensible choices and the right costs, including "on average" for the hash set and "amortised" for the vector. Two alternatives are as good: a sorted
of pairs for task 3, if the parameters are loaded once and never change, and a ring buffer over a
for task 5, if the queue has a fixed bound. One or two wrong costs or missing reasons are a partial pass. A
without a reason that needs one, or more than two misses, is a fail.

STL, the standard template library, is the part of C++ that gives you containers: types that store a collection of objects and promise a fixed cost for reading, inserting and erasing them. Those costs come from how a container lays out its elements. A
keep every element in one heap block; a
keeps them in fixed blocks reached through a table of pointers;
keep each element in its own node, linked into a sorted tree;
keep each element in its own node too, reached through a hash and a bucket.
needs no heap, because its element count is part of its type, so the elements sit inside the object.
The problem is that the wrong choice quietly costs a robot cycles, or memory, it didn't need to spend. A
has no O(1) way to drop its own front element, because everything behind it has to shift left. A hash table like
answers "is this key present" fast but can't answer "which key comes right before this one" without checking every entry, a question only a sorted tree answers directly.

The mechanism behind the choice is what each layout makes cheap. One contiguous block gives O(1) access by index and the fastest walk, because the processor can prefetch what comes next, so it wins whenever you read sequentially or by position. A tree keeps every search, insert and erase at O(log n) by staying balanced, paid for with a node and three pointers per element. A hash table trades that order for O(1) lookup on average, built from a hash function and buckets.

What it costs to default to a tree or a hash table everywhere is memory: a node adds pointers and an allocation per element that a plain block never spends, which is why the Core Guidelines default to
up to a few kilobytes. What it costs to always reach for a vector is the operations its layout can't do cheaply, such as an insert at the front or a lookup by key.
You meet this choice built into the robot at every turn:
for four wheel speeds fixed at compile time,
for a route walked start to end,
for parameters a status page prints in order,
for message ids you only ever ask "have I seen this" about. That is the interview question itself, asked as five small tasks and a cost for each.

is the same tree holding keys without values.

answers only exact questions: is this key present, and what is its value? It answers them in O(1) on average and O(n) at worst, and it iterates in no useful order. The DSA topic on hash maps shows how buckets give that average and how colliding keys give the worst case, so this topic doesn't repeat it. Choose by the questions you need to ask. Nearest, first, last, a range of keys or sorted output need a tree. Exact lookups alone need a hash table, or, for a few dozen entries, a sorted vector.
